content: Epizootic lymphangitis is a contagious disease affecting the lymphatic system of horses and mules, caused by the fungal organism Histoplasma farciminosum. While cattle can also contract the disease, they exhibit a higher level of resistance compared to equids. In the United Kingdom, epizootic lymphangitis is classified as a notifiable disease, meaning its occurrence must be reported to authorities. The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) categorizes it as a List B disease, which includes transmissible diseases of socio-economic and/or public health importance that also have significant implications for international trade in animals and animal products. Reports on such diseases are typically submitted annually. The clinical presentation of epizootic lymphangitis often includes the following symptoms: Skin eruptions, primarily on the legs, though they may occasionally appear on the head or neck and rarely on other parts of the body. Prominent lymphatic vessels in the affected skin, accompanied by small, firm nodules approximately 1 cm in diameter along their course. These nodules tend to suppurate, forming abscesses that discharge thick, yellow pus. Over time, granulation tissue (proud flesh) develops from the wounds, with surrounding lymphatic vessels becoming inflamed. The skin eruptions gradually spread. Neighboring lymph nodes become swollen and firm. The ulcers are slow to heal, even with treatment, and may recur after an apparent resolution. Diagnosis of epizootic lymphangitis is distinguished from glanders (also known as farcy) by identifying Histoplasma organisms in the pus and the absence of a reaction to the mallein test. It is worth noting that both glanders and epizootic lymphangitis can coexist in the same animal. Serological testing can also aid in confirming the diagnosis. Control of the disease typically involves eliminating the source of infection. This is achieved by culling infected horses and implementing strict hygiene measures to prevent the spread of the fungal organism. Vaccination has been used in some regions, such as Iraq, but it is not authorized for widespread use.
